lead: A clipper removes the part of a waveform that lies above or below a chosen level. A clamper moves the whole waveform up or down without changing its peak-to-peak value. Both use a diode as a switch. A clipper uses a battery (or Zener) to set the clip level; a clamper uses a capacitor to store the DC shift and a diode returned to a reference. They protect inputs, reshape signals and set DC levels in radios, sensors and audio gear. Some syllabi call clippers limiting circuits. A sensor input that must not see a spike above 4 V, for example, uses a clipper. The next sections show the circuits, their transfer characteristics and the time-constant rule for clampers.
prereq: You need: the diode switch model and sine-wave peak values from Chapter 1.1, plus the RC time constant from Chapter 1.2.

blocks.text: A clipper is a diode network that passes one part of the input and cuts the rest. In a shunt clipper the diode sits across the output. When it conducts, it holds the output at a reference level. In a series clipper the diode sits in the signal path. When it is off, no signal reaches the output. The diode acts as a switch: about 0.7 V forward drop for silicon, open in reverse, or 0 V in the ideal model.
V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>ref</sub> + V<sub>D</sub>   (diode on, shunt clipper)
blocks.where: V<sub>ref</sub> is the battery reference voltage in volts; V<sub>D</sub> is the diode forward drop, about 0.7 V for silicon and 0 V for an ideal diode.

blocks.text: A bias battery sets the clip level. A positive clipper removes positive peaks above V<sub>ref</sub>. A negative clipper removes negative peaks below −V<sub>ref</sub>. Reversing the diode or the battery changes which peak is cut and at what level. Two branches make a double clipper that cuts both peaks.

items: Positive shunt clipper: output is flat at V<sub>ref</sub> + V<sub>D</sub> (≈ V<sub>ref</sub> + 0.7 V with a silicon diode) when V<sub>in</sub> is above it.
Negative shunt clipper: output is flat at −(V<sub>ref</sub> + V<sub>D</sub>) when V<sub>in</sub> is below it.
Biased clipper: the battery moves the clip level away from zero.
Double clipper: one branch cuts the top, the other cuts the bottom.

blocks.text: These levels assume the diode is on. V<sub>ref</sub> alone is the level only for an ideal diode.
The transfer characteristic plots V<sub>out</sub> against V<sub>in</sub>. Inside the pass region the slope is 1. On a clipped peak the slope is 0, so the curve is flat.

A clamper, also called a DC restorer, uses a capacitor in series with the signal and a diode to a reference. On the first half-cycle the diode conducts and charges the capacitor to the peak of the input minus the diode drop. Then the diode turns off and the capacitor holds that voltage. The output is the input plus the capacitor voltage, so the whole waveform shifts. The peak-to-peak value does not change; the average value does.
V<sub>C</sub> = V<sub>p</sub> − V<sub>D</sub> ;   V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>in</sub> + V<sub>C</sub>
blocks.where: V<sub>C</sub> is the capacitor voltage in volts; V<sub>p</sub> is the input peak in volts; V<sub>D</sub> is the diode drop in volts. Use V<sub>C</sub> ≈ −(V<sub>p</sub> − V<sub>D</sub>) for a negative clamper.

blocks.text: A positive clamper pushes the waveform upward so its negative peak sits near 0 V. With an ideal diode and a 10 V peak sine, the output swings from 0 V to +20 V. A negative clamper pushes the waveform downward so its positive peak sits near 0 V, swinging from −20 V to 0 V.

The capacitor must hold its charge during the whole cycle. Choose the load resistance R<sub>L</sub> and capacitance C so that R<sub>L</sub>C is much larger than the period T. A common design rule is R<sub>L</sub>C ≥ 10T, where T = 1/f. If the time constant is too small, the output droops or tilts.

A real diode turns on gradually near 0.7 V, so a clipper corner is rounded rather than sharp. Above the knee the diode has a small resistance, so the clipped top is not perfectly flat. A clamper output also loses about 0.7 V because of the diode drop. The capacitor must be connected with the polarity that matches its charging voltage; an electrolytic capacitor placed the wrong way can fail.

Check a clipper by comparing the output peak with the reference level. Check a clamper by comparing peak-to-peak values: they must be equal at input and output. The average output equals the average input plus VC. Clampers are used as DC restorers in video and as level shifters before ADCs. Clippers protect RF mixers and comparator inputs. For precision clipping, op-amp circuits appear in Unit 6; Zener limiting is covered in Chapter 1.4.

figure.caption: A 10 V peak sine input and the output of a shunt positive clipper with a 4 V reference and an ideal diode. The positive peaks are flat at +4 V; the negative half-cycle passes unchanged.

spec.aria: Plot of a 10 V sine input and its output clipped at +4 V; the output is flat at +4 V on positive peaks.

examples.question: A 10 V peak, 50 Hz sine wave drives a shunt positive clipper with an ideal diode in series with a 4 V battery. The diode conducts when the input exceeds 4 V. Sketch the input and output for one cycle and state the output peak-to-peak voltage.
steps: Input peak V<sub>p</sub> = 10 V. Input minimum = −10 V. Input peak-to-peak = 10 − (−10) = 20 V.
The battery reference is 4 V and the diode is ideal, so the clip level is 4 V.
When V<sub>in</sub> > 4 V, the diode conducts and V<sub>out</sub> = 4 V. This starts at θ = sin<sup>−1</sup>(4/10) = 23.6° and ends at 180° − 23.6° = 156.4°.
When V<sub>in</sub> ≤ 4 V, the diode is off and V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>in</sub>. The negative peak reaches −10 V.
Output maximum = +4 V. Output minimum = −10 V. Output peak-to-peak = 4 − (−10) = 14 V.
examples.answer: The output peak-to-peak voltage is 14 V.
examples.check:
vp = 10.0
vref = 4.0
vmin = -vp
pp = vref - vmin
print(pp)

traps: Reversing the diode changes the clipper from positive to negative; reversing the battery moves the clip level but does not change the peak that is cut.
A clamper changes the DC average but never the peak-to-peak value; an answer that reports a smaller peak-to-peak for an ideal clamper is wrong.
A practical clamper output is shifted by about 0.7 V less than the ideal value because of the diode drop.
If R<sub>L</sub>C is not much larger than T, the capacitor discharges and the clamped waveform droops or tilts.
In a shunt clipper the diode conducts and shorts the output to the reference; in a series clipper the diode opens the signal path. Do not mix the two.

quiz.q: Define a clipper and a clamper in one line each.
quiz.a: A clipper removes part of a waveform above or below a set level. A clamper shifts the whole waveform in DC level without changing its peak-to-peak value.

quiz.q: Why does an ideal clamper not change the peak-to-peak value of a sine wave?
quiz.a: The capacitor adds a fixed DC voltage to every point of the waveform. The distance between the maximum and minimum therefore stays the same; only the average moves.

quiz.q: A 10 V peak sine drives a shunt positive clipper with an ideal diode and a 3 V battery. Find the output maximum, minimum and peak-to-peak voltage.
quiz.a: Output maximum = +3 V. Output minimum = −10 V. Peak-to-peak = 3 − (−10) = 13 V.

quiz.q: A clamper uses R<sub>L</sub> = 1 kΩ and C = 0.1 μF at 50 Hz. Find R<sub>L</sub>C and state whether the clamping is good.
quiz.a: R<sub>L</sub>C = 1000 × 0.1 × 10<sup>−6</sup> = 1 × 10<sup>−4</sup> s = 0.1 ms. T = 20 ms. Since R<sub>L</sub>C is much smaller than T, the capacitor discharges quickly and the clamping is poor; the output droops.
A plot of output voltage against input voltage for a circuit, showing the pass region and the clipped flat regions.

quiz.q: Give one difference between a series clipper and a shunt clipper.
quiz.a: In a shunt clipper the diode is across the output and shorts the output to a reference when it conducts. In a series clipper the diode is in the signal path and blocks the signal when it is off.

quiz.q: The diode in a positive clamper is reversed by mistake. What happens to the output?
quiz.a: The capacitor charges with the opposite polarity. The waveform is shifted downward instead of upward, so the positive peak sits near 0 V and the negative peak goes to about −20 V for a 10 V peak input.

beyond: Not for the exam. Diode clippers appear in RF front ends as limiters that protect mixers from strong nearby transmitters. Clampers are used in video systems to restore the DC level lost after AC coupling. In IC design, ESD protection networks use diode clamps at input pads. Search next for “diode clipper transfer characteristic”, “clamper time constant”, and “precision clipper op-amp”. Op-amp precision clippers and peak detectors are developed in Unit 6.
